title: When It Does Not Make Sense
subtitle: A five-session study on suffering, lament, and the God who does not explain.
summary:
This study is for people in pain, for the ones sitting near them who have run out of things to say, and for the small groups willing to hold a hard question without rushing to close it. It walks slowly through five sessions on the problem of pain stated at full weight, on lament as faithful speech rather than faithlessness, on the cross as the place God answered suffering by entering it instead of explaining it, on the slow work endurance does without ever becoming a formula, and on the new creation where every tear is finally wiped away by the hand of God himself. It refuses the cheap answers the church reaches for out of its own discomfort, the everything happens for a reason and the God needed another angel, and it refuses just as firmly the despair that reads a wound as proof there is no one there. It is built so a person with no training can lead it, because every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than in the argument grief was already having on the drive over.

This is not a study that stands above suffering and dispenses answers. The writer came to faith out of atheism, was raised without a father, and has buried people he loved and sat with people who wanted to die, and he does not point at pain from a safe distance. He has prayed the prayer that was answered with silence. He has offered a grieving person the sentence he later wished he could take back. He writes from inside the room where the question why has no floor under it. So will you. And there is one thing this study will not do, ever. It will not tell a person in agony that the answer is simply to trust more, or that their grief is a failure of faith, or that God is fine with them staying in a darkness that is putting their life at risk. Where the pain has turned toward self-harm or despair that will not lift, the study says plainly that this is the moment to reach for a pastor, a counselor, a doctor, or a crisis line, and to reach today. The gospel does not require anyone to suffer alone. The God at the center of this study is the one who wept at a grave he was about to open.
audience: Anyone in grief or pain, those walking with them, and small groups

sessions.title: The Question We Are Not Allowed to Ask
sessions.aim: To state the problem of pain at its full weight rather than defusing it early, to honor the protest tradition of Job and the psalmists who put the hard question to God directly, and to refuse both the atheism that treats suffering as a closed case against God and the false piety that will not let a sufferer say why.
sessions.summary: A woman sat across from Bell a week after her husband's funeral and said the thing people are not supposed to say in a church, that she did not want comfort, she wanted an explanation, and that if God had one she would like to hear it now. He did not have one to give her. The instinct in that moment is to reach for a sentence that makes the ache smaller, and the church has a drawer full of them, everything happens for a reason, God needed another angel, he will not give you more than you can handle. Every one of them is a way of not letting the person ask the question. The real question is not whether suffering is hard but whether it is permitted to be spoken plainly to God, and Scripture's answer is startling, because the Bible does not flinch from the problem, it wrote the sharpest version of it into its own pages. Job loses everything for no reason the sufferer is ever told, and then spends thirty-eight chapters refusing the tidy theology of his friends and demanding that God answer him to his face. Bell takes the strong case for the atheist here, the one he once made himself, that a world with this much undeserved agony in it is hard to square with a God who is both good and able. There is real weight in it, and the friends who explained Job's pain were rebuked by God while Job, who protested, was commended. But the atheist case proves less than it claims, because the same suffering that looks like an argument against God is, in Job, the occasion for meeting him. God never gives Job the explanation. He gives Job himself. And Job, who had demanded answers, says at the end that he had heard of God by the hearing of the ear but now his eye sees him, and lays his hand over his mouth. The problem of pain is real. This study will not shrink it. But the God it points to did not send an argument into the world. He came in person, and he came weeping.

keyScripture.why: Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face, holding together in one breath the trust that keeps holding on and the protest that refuses to pretend, and modeling the faith that is honest enough to bring its accusation straight to God.

discussion.q: Bell says the church keeps a drawer full of sentences that make the ache smaller, everything happens for a reason and the rest. Which one has been said to you in your pain, and what did it actually do?
discussion.behind: Open on the real experience, not the theory. Almost everyone in the room has been handed one of these lines in a hard season, and most will admit it landed as dismissal even when it was meant as care. The point is not to mock the people who said them, most were frightened and kind, but to name honestly that the cliche is usually a way of ending the conversation the sufferer most needed to have. Let the room be honest before anyone defends the sayings.

discussion.q: Job's friends explained his suffering and were rebuked by God, while Job, who protested and demanded answers, was commended. What does it change to learn that God preferred the protest to the explanation?
discussion.behind: Get under the assumption that faith means never questioning. The book of Job is God's own verdict on this, and the verdict is surprising, because the men who defended God with tidy theology are the ones told they have not spoken rightly. Help the room feel the permission in that, that honest anguish addressed to God is not the opposite of faith but a form of it, while the neat defense of God can be its own kind of unbelief.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case for the atheist, that a world with this much undeserved agony is hard to square with a good and able God. What is true in that objection that you do not want to lose?
discussion.behind: Protect the honesty of the hard case, and do not let the room rush to answer it. This is the strongest argument against the faith, and a study that will not state it fairly has not earned the right to respond. The truth in it is real, suffering is genuinely a problem and pretending otherwise is dishonest. Make sure the skeptic in the room, or the believer with a skeptic's ache, hears the objection taken seriously before anyone offers a word back.

discussion.q: God never gives Job the explanation he demanded, only himself, and Job goes quiet. Why do you think presence satisfied Job when an answer might not have, and have you ever known that to be true?
discussion.behind: This is the theological center of the session. The book withholds the reason on purpose and gives the sufferer God instead, and Job, who wanted an argument, is undone by an encounter. Do not resolve too fast, because for many in the room the answer still has not come and presence has not yet felt like enough. Let them hold the tension. Point only toward the possibility that what the heart in agony most needs is not information but company.

discussion.q: Bell says he has offered a grieving person a sentence he later wished he could take back. Where have you reached for a cheap answer to ease your own discomfort with someone else's pain?
discussion.behind: Move from diagnosis to self-implication, and go first. Everyone in the room has done this, has filled a hard silence with a platitude to make themselves less uncomfortable near another person's grief. The point is not shame but honesty, because you cannot sit well with a sufferer until you have admitted how often you have fled their pain by explaining it. Confess your own before you ask anyone to confess theirs.

objections.objection: The amount of pointless, undeserved suffering in the world is the clearest evidence there is no good God. A God who could stop a child's agony and does not is either not good or not real, and no amount of theology closes that gap.
objections.response: Sit with the weight of it, because this is the strongest thing the unbeliever says and it deserves no flinching. The suffering is real, much of it is undeserved, and any answer that makes it small is not an answer but an evasion, and the Bible itself refuses that evasion by writing Job. Grant all of that without hedging. Then notice what the objection quietly assumes, that if there were a good God he would owe us an explanation we could follow. But the book of Job, which stares at exactly this problem, does not end by explaining the suffering. It ends by God arriving, and the sufferer discovering that the deepest human need in agony was never the reason but the presence. The atheist case is right that suffering is a genuine problem. Where it overreaches is in assuming a problem we cannot solve must mean there is no one there, when the Christian claim is stranger and harder, that the one who is there did not stay above the problem but entered it, and hung inside it, on a cross.

objections.objection: Telling people to just trust God and stop asking why is exactly how the church silences hurting people and makes their grief feel like a sin. Questioning God is treated as weak faith, when it may be the most honest thing a person can do.
objections.response: Grant this fully, because the church has often done precisely what it describes, and the harm is real. Hurting people have been made to feel that their questions were faithlessness, that a good Christian grieves quietly and never asks why, and that pressure has driven honest sufferers either into pretending or out the door. That instinct is not from Scripture, it is from the church's own discomfort. The Bible does the opposite. It hands us Job, who argues his case to God's face and is commended for it, and a book of Psalms where a third of the songs are complaints, and a Savior who cried out on the cross asking why he was forsaken. So the honest question is not a threat to faith, it is often the truest form of it, the refusal to make peace with a lie in order to look pious. What the study does insist is that the question be aimed at God rather than away from him, brought into the relationship rather than used to end it, because Job kept talking to the God he was arguing with, and that is the difference between lament and leaving.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the question about your own suffering, or someone you love, that you have never let yourself ask God out loud, and what are you afraid would happen if you did?
sessions.practice: This week, take the question you have been keeping from God, the why you have swallowed to seem faithful, and say it to him directly, out loud or on paper, without softening it into something more acceptable. Do not answer it for him and do not apologize for it. Just bring it into the room with him the way Job did. And notice, when you have said it, whether the honesty pushed you further from God or, strangely, closer. Write down what you actually felt when the real question was finally spoken.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have been taught to hide our hardest questions from you, as though you were too fragile or too far to hear them, and so we have carried them alone and called our silence trust. Forgive us the cheap answers we have handed to people in pain because their grief frightened us. Forgive us the platitudes we have used to end conversations you wanted to hold. Teach us to bring the real question to you the way Job did, to his face, and to discover that you would rather have our honest anguish than our polished distance. Where any of us is in a darkness that has grown dangerous, do not let us hide it. Send us people with hands, and help us reach for them today. And meet us, as you met Job, not with an argument but with yourself. Amen.
reflection: What cheap answer to suffering have I believed or repeated, and what has it kept me from feeling honestly, in myself or with others?
Do I actually believe God can bear my hardest question, or have I been protecting him, and myself, by never asking it?
When I am near someone in real pain, do I sit with them in it, or do I reach for a sentence that makes me more comfortable and them more alone?
sessions.teaching: A woman sat across from Bell a week after burying her husband and said the sentence you are not supposed to say inside a church. She said she did not want comfort. She wanted an explanation, and if God had one, she would like to hear it now. He did not have one to give her, and the honest thing was to say so and stay in the chair rather than reach for something to fill the silence. Because there is an instinct, in that moment, to make the ache smaller, and the church has a whole drawer of sentences built for exactly that. Everything happens for a reason. God needed another angel. He will not give you more than you can handle. God has a plan. Every one of those sayings, however kindly meant, does the same quiet thing. It ends the conversation the sufferer most needed to have. It hands them a lid for a grief that was asking to be seen. So we begin here, not with an answer to suffering but with permission to ask about it, because the real question is not whether pain is hard, everyone in the room already knows it is hard. The real question is whether the pain is allowed to be spoken plainly to God, and the Bible's answer to that will surprise anyone who was raised to think faith means never questioning. Scripture does not flinch from the problem of pain. It wrote the sharpest version of that problem into its own pages and put it in the canon. His name is Job. A man loses his children, his health, his wealth, everything but his life and a wife who tells him to curse God and die, and the reader is let in on a secret the sufferer never learns, that there is no sin behind it, no lesson he failed, no reason he is ever told. And then Job does the thing that should reorder how we think a believer is supposed to behave. He refuses the tidy theology of his friends, who keep insisting that suffering must be deserved, that if he would just repent the pain would lift, that God is fair in the way they can diagram. And Job argues. For chapter after chapter he protests, he demands, he says he will hold on to God and argue his ways to God's face in the same breath. Take the strong case for the other side now, the atheist's case, because I once made it myself before I believed any of this, and it deserves to be stated at full strength rather than knocked down as a cartoon. The case is simple and it is heavy. A world with this much undeserved agony in it, this much suffering that teaches nothing and redeems nothing and falls on the innocent, is genuinely hard to square with a God who is at once perfectly good and fully able to stop it. If he can and will not, is he good. If he would and cannot, is he God. That is not a stupid question. It is one of the oldest and most serious questions a human being can ask, and any faith that will not take it seriously is not worth having. Grant its weight. And notice, before we go further, that the book of Job grants it too, because at the end God speaks, and he is angry, and his anger falls not on Job who protested but on the friends who explained. They defended God with neat answers and God tells them they have not spoken of him what is right, while Job, who shook his fist and demanded a hearing, is the one commended. Let that land, because it overturns a lifetime of bad teaching. God preferred the honest protest to the tidy defense. He would rather have the man who argued with him than the men who explained him. But here is where the atheist case, real as its weight is, proves less than it claims. It assumes that a problem we cannot solve must mean there is no one there. And the strange thing about Job is that the suffering which looked like an argument against God became the occasion for meeting him. Because God does answer Job, out of the whirlwind, and what is astonishing is what the answer is not. It is not an explanation. God never tells Job about the wager, never gives him the reason, never diagrams the fairness his friends kept trying to defend. God gives Job something else. God gives Job himself, page after page of presence, the sheer overwhelming reality of the One who made leviathan and laid the foundations of the earth. And Job, who had demanded answers, says at the last that he had heard of God by the hearing of the ear, but now his eye sees him, and he lays his hand over his mouth. Not because he was bullied into silence. Because he was met. I have to stand inside this, because I have been the friend more than I have been Job. I have sat beside real grief and reached for the sentence that made me more comfortable and the other person more alone. I have explained a pain that only needed company. The temptation to answer is almost always the temptation to flee, to fix the ache so I do not have to feel it with you. And the gospel underneath this whole study is that God did the opposite of what I keep doing. He did not send an explanation into the suffering of the world. He came into it in person. He came and stood at a grave he was about to open, and before he opened it, he wept.

scriptureStudy.note: The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. Job's first response is worship, not because he understood, but before he understood, which is neither denial nor despair. The book will not let this be his last word, but it refuses to let it be nothing.

Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire. The same man who worshiped now curses the day he was born, and Scripture puts both on the page without embarrassment. Faith and this raw wish that he had never lived are allowed to sit in the same person.

Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face. This is the hinge of the book, trust and protest in a single sentence. Job will not let go of God and will not pretend he is fine, and the Bible calls that faith.

Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? God's answer begins not with the reason for Job's pain but with a flood of questions Job cannot answer, relocating him from the center of the universe to a creature before his Maker, which is somehow the comfort.

I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. Job never gets his explanation. He gets an encounter, and it is enough, because the deepest need of the sufferer turned out to be presence and not information.

My anger burns against you, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has. God rebukes the friends who defended him with tidy theology and vindicates the man who protested, overturning the assumption that questioning God is faithlessness.

In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider. The Preacher refuses the formula that would let us read prosperity as reward and adversity as punishment, insisting that God has made the one as well as the other and hidden the reasons from us.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the long history the session only gestures at, because the problem of pain has a genealogy worth knowing, and the modern form of it is younger than most people assume. The word theodicy, the justification of God in the face of evil, was coined by the philosopher Gottfried Leibniz in a work published in 1710, in which he argued that ours is the best of all possible worlds. A group can weigh how confident, and how brittle, that optimism was, because it did not survive the century. On the first of November in 1755 an earthquake destroyed Lisbon on a holy day while the churches were full, and the shock to the European conscience was so great that Voltaire turned it into a weapon against exactly Leibniz's optimism, first in a poem and then in the merciless satire of Candide. The point for a Christian group is not to take sides between the philosopher and the skeptic, both of whom were trying to solve suffering as an equation, but to notice that the book of Job had already refused the equation two and a half millennia earlier, neither defending God with a formula nor abandoning him for the lack of one. Set this beside C. S. Lewis, who wrote The Problem of Pain in 1940 as a careful intellectual defense of God in the face of suffering, and then, twenty years later, having watched his wife die of cancer, wrote A Grief Observed, a raw journal that reads at times like it is arguing with the earlier book. A group should sit with that pairing honestly, because it shows something true, that an answer that satisfies the mind in the study can shatter at the graveside, and that the God who meets us in grief is finally a person to be encountered and not a proposition to be proved. Then take the hardest turn, and take it with care for the wounded in the room. The temptation for a thoughtful group is to treat suffering as a puzzle to be solved rather than a wound to be borne, and to leave the session feeling intellectually satisfied while the actual sufferer feels more alone. Refuse that. The aim of this session is not to win the argument about pain. It is to recover the permission Job was given, to bring the real question to God, and to learn to sit beside a hurting person the way God sat with Job, in overwhelming presence rather than tidy explanation.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group is the fixer, the one who cannot bear an unresolved problem, and when another member shares a raw and unanswered grief, he immediately offers reasons, God is working this for good, there must be a purpose, at least it was not worse. He is not cruel, and he genuinely wants to help, and he believes offering answers is love. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor him before it corrects him. His desire to help is real and good, and the impulse to comfort is not the problem. But notice what his answers are actually doing, because the reasons he offers are closing a door the grieving person needed left open, and every explanation lands as a quiet instruction to stop feeling what they feel. He is being Job's friend, the very role God rebuked, defending God with a formula while the sufferer needed only to be heard. Do not shame him, because most of the room has done exactly what he is doing. Help him see the difference between fixing a pain and bearing it with someone, and ask him, gently, whether his answers are for the sufferer's comfort or for his own, whether he is sitting in the ash heap beside his friend or standing over it with a solution. The most loving thing he can learn to do is to stay, and to say less.

sessions.title: Permission to Complain to God
sessions.aim: To recover lament as faithful speech rather than a lapse of faith, to see that a third of the Psalms train the church to bring its grief and its accusation directly to God, and to refuse the false piety that mistakes a forced brightness for trust and drives honest sorrow underground.
sessions.summary: Bell says the most dishonest hour of the week is often the one on Sunday morning, when a room full of people carrying real griefs agrees to sing as though none of them were there. He does not mean the singing is wrong. He means the church has quietly taught its people that faith sounds only one way, upbeat and resolved, and that sorrow brought into worship is a kind of failure. The real question is what the Bible actually gives us to pray when life caves in, and the answer is embarrassing to a church that has forgotten it, because roughly a third of the Psalms, the songbook God gave his people, are laments. They are complaints. They are the accusations and the questions and the raw grief of people who kept talking to God precisely when they were furious with him. How long, O Lord. Why have you forsaken me. Will you forget me forever. These are not the prayers of weak faith. They are Scripture, put in our mouths on purpose. Bell takes the strong case for the other side, that constant complaint is corrosive, that a grateful heart is healthier than a grievance, that some people use their pain as a permanent excuse. There is truth in it, and the study will name the difference between lament and mere grumbling. But the pious alternative, the smile that will not admit the wound, is not trust. It is often just fear wearing trust's clothes, the terror that God cannot handle the truth of us. Then the reversal. The psalms of lament almost always turn, not to a fixed problem but to a remembered God, and the turn comes only because the complaint was allowed to be fully spoken first. You cannot arrive at trust by skipping the sorrow. You get there through it, saying the whole terrible thing to the God who wrote the words down for you to say.

keyScripture.why: How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? modeling the lament that accuses God to his face and keeps addressing him in the same breath, and proving that this raw complaint is not the failure of faith but its scripted and sanctioned speech.

discussion.q: Bell says the church has quietly taught people that faith sounds only one way, upbeat and resolved, so that sorrow in worship feels like failure. Where have you felt you had to hide your grief to seem faithful?
discussion.behind: Open on the lived pressure, gently, because many carry it without ever naming it. The unspoken rule that a good Christian is always fine has kept countless people performing a wholeness they do not feel. Help the room admit the gap between the face they bring to church and the ache they carry in, and let the honesty itself begin to break the rule.

discussion.q: A third of the Psalms are laments, complaints God put in his people's mouths on purpose. What does it change to learn that How long, O Lord and Why have you forsaken me are Scripture, not faithlessness?
discussion.behind: Get under the assumption that complaint to God is sin. Most in the room have never been told that the Bible's own prayer book is soaked in protest, and the news is freeing. Help them feel that God did not just tolerate these prayers, he authored them and handed them to us to pray, which means the sorrow they have been hiding has a scriptural voice waiting for it.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that constant complaint is corrosive and a grateful heart is healthier. What is true in that, and where is the line between faithful lament and mere grumbling?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves honestly. There is a real difference between lament and grumbling, and the study should not pretend otherwise. The clue is direction, lament is spoken to God and keeps holding on to him, while grumbling is spoken about God, to others, and lets go. Help the room locate the line without using it to shame anyone back into silence, because the greater danger in most churches is not too much lament but far too little.

discussion.q: The psalms of lament almost always turn toward a remembered God, but only after the complaint is fully spoken. Why do you think the turn comes through the sorrow rather than around it?
discussion.behind: This is the theological center. The lament psalms do not skip the grief to reach the hope, they move through the grief and the hope is on the other side of the honesty. Help the room see that you cannot shortcut to trust by suppressing sorrow, that the psalmist reaches the remembered faithfulness of God precisely because he was first allowed to say the whole terrible thing. Do not rush the turn. Honor the complaint first.

discussion.q: Bell says the forced smile is often fear wearing trust's clothes, the terror that God cannot handle the truth of us. Where has your brightness been protecting you from being fully honest with God?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication, and go first. Many perform a settled faith not out of trust but out of a quiet fear that the real anger and doubt would be too much, that God might turn away if he saw it all. Name your own version of this. Help the room see that hiding from God is not reverence, it is distance, and that the psalmists honored God more by telling him everything than we do by telling him only the acceptable parts.

objections.objection: The Bible tells us to give thanks in all circumstances and to rejoice always. All this permission to complain sounds like it just baptizes self-pity and lets people wallow instead of trusting God.
objections.response: Grant the verses, because they are real and they are commands, and a life of endless grievance is a genuine spiritual danger that Scripture warns against, and gratitude really is a healthier and truer posture than a permanent grudge. Hold all of that. But notice that the same Bible that says rejoice always gave us a prayer book a third full of laments, which means these cannot be contradictions, they must be two things held together. The difference is not between complaint and gratitude, it is between grumbling and lament. Grumbling talks about God to other people and slowly lets go of him. Lament talks to God, keeps holding on to him, and almost always turns, in the end, toward remembered faithfulness. The psalmist who cries how long is not wallowing, he is doing the hard work of dragging his whole grief into the presence of God rather than nursing it in the dark. And here is the thing self-pity can never do that lament does. Self-pity ends in the self. Lament ends in God. Rejoicing always is not the denial of the sorrow, it is what you find on the far side of having spoken it honestly to the only One who can bear it.

objections.objection: If I really trusted God, I would not need to complain to him at all. Bringing him my anger and my questions just shows my faith is weak, and I should be able to accept his will without all the protest.
objections.response: Hear the reverence underneath this, because it is trying to honor God, and that instinct is not nothing. But it rests on a picture of faith the Bible simply does not share. If bringing God your anguish were a sign of weak faith, then Job had weak faith, and the psalmists had weak faith, and Jeremiah in his Lamentations had weak faith, and Jesus himself, crying from the cross the opening line of a lament psalm, had weak faith, which is impossible. The truth runs the other way. It takes more faith, not less, to bring God your fury than to bury it, because burying it assumes he cannot be trusted with the real you. The person who protests to God is still talking to God, still inside the relationship, still holding on. The greater danger to faith is not the honest complaint, it is the polite distance that decides certain things are too true to say to him, and so slowly stops saying anything at all. Accepting God's will is real and good, but it is the destination the lament psalms travel toward, not a shortcut that skips the honesty. You reach acceptance through the protest, not instead of it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the grief or the anger you have been bringing to everyone except God, and what would it mean to say the whole of it to him, in the words of a lament, this week?
sessions.practice: This week, pray a lament psalm as your own, slowly, out loud if you can. Take Psalm 13, or 22, or the unrelenting darkness of Psalm 88, and let the words carry the grief you have not known how to say, including the parts that accuse. Do not skip to the turn at the end until you have meant the complaint at the beginning. If your own honest lament is longer than the psalm, keep going in your own words, but keep addressing God. Write down what happened in you when Scripture itself gave you permission to say the hard thing.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we have brought you our best manners and hidden our worst grief, as though you were a guest to be impressed rather than a Father who already sees. Forgive us the forced brightness we mistook for trust. Forgive us for teaching one another that faith may only sound one way, and for the sorrows we have driven underground because the room had no place for them. Thank you that you wrote our complaints into your own book and put them in our mouths, that how long and why are words you gave us and not sins you punish. Teach us to lament, to say the whole terrible thing to you and keep holding on, and to find, on the far side of the honesty, the God who was faithful all along. And where a sorrow has grown too heavy to carry alone, give us the courage to let another person in. Amen.
reflection: Where have I performed a settled faith I did not feel, and what has that performance cost me in honesty with God and with others?
Do I know the difference, in my own heart, between lament that keeps holding on to God and grumbling that quietly lets go of him?
What would change if I believed God would rather have my furious, honest prayer than my polite and distant one?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the most dishonest hour of many people's week is Sunday morning, when a room full of people carrying real and heavy griefs quietly agrees to sing as though none of those griefs were in the building. He is careful about what he means. The singing is not the problem, and the joy is not fake in everyone. What he means is that the church has, over generations, taught its people a lie about what faith is allowed to sound like, that it sounds upbeat, resolved, grateful, settled, and that sorrow brought into worship is a kind of leak, a failure of the trust everyone is supposed to have arrived already possessing. So people learn to leave their grief in the car. They learn to answer fine. They learn that the acceptable Christian emotions are a short list and theirs are not on it. And the real question underneath all of this is a simple one that the church has strangely forgotten how to answer. What does the Bible actually give us to pray when our life caves in. Not what should we feel, not how quickly should we recover, but what words does God himself put in our mouths for the day the diagnosis comes, or the child does not, or the marriage ends, or the prayer is met with nothing at all. And the answer is genuinely embarrassing to a church that has forgotten it, because the answer is lament. Roughly a third of the Psalms, the songbook God gave his own people for their worship, are laments. They are complaints. They are the raw, unedited grief and anger and confusion of people who kept talking to God precisely at the moments they were most furious with him. How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever. My God, my God, why have you forsaken me. Why do you hide your face. These are not the prayers of people with weak faith who needed to be corrected. They are Scripture. God inspired them, preserved them, and handed them to us on purpose, which means that the sorrow you have been taught to hide has a voice in the Bible waiting for you to use it. Take the strong case for the other side, because it is real and I do not want to wave it away. There is such a thing as corrosive complaint. There are people who take a genuine wound and build a permanent identity out of it, who talk about their grievance until it becomes the only thing they are, who use their pain as a standing excuse to be unkind. Scripture warns about grumbling repeatedly and it means it, and a grateful heart really is healthier and truer than a bitter one. Grant all of that. But watch the crucial distinction, because everything turns on it. The difference is not between complaint and gratitude. It is between grumbling and lament, and they are not the same thing at all. Grumbling talks about God, to other people, in the dark, and it slowly lets go of him. Lament talks to God, to his face, and it holds on. The grumbler walks away narrating his complaint to anyone who will listen. The lamenter walks toward God with the very same complaint and refuses to leave. And the pious alternative that most churches actually offer, the fixed smile that will not admit the wound is even there, is not the opposite of grumbling. It is not trust at all, most of the time. It is fear wearing trust's clothing, the quiet terror that if God saw the real anger, the real doubt, the real fury underneath, he would turn away, and so we show him only the parts we think he can stand. I know that fear from the inside. There have been seasons I prayed carefully, offering God a managed and acceptable version of myself, because the true version felt too dangerous to say out loud, and all the while I called that reticence reverence. It was not reverence. It was distance. Now here is the reversal that the lament psalms teach, and it is the whole point of the session. The laments almost always turn. Read them and you will see it, Psalm 13 begins with how long and forget me forever and ends with I will sing to the Lord because he has dealt bountifully with me. But watch how the turn comes, because it does not come by fixing the problem. Nothing external changes between the first verse and the last. The turn comes by remembering the God the complaint is addressed to, and, crucially, it comes only after the complaint has been fully and honestly spoken. The psalmist does not skip the sorrow to reach the hope. He goes through the sorrow and the hope is waiting on the other side of the honesty. This is the thing the forced smile can never do. You cannot arrive at trust by suppressing the grief. You get there through it. And the darkest lament of all, Psalm 88, does not even turn, it ends with the word darkness, and God left it in the book anyway, which is his own quiet promise that even the prayer that finds no light is still a prayer he receives. So we are being invited to a harder and better honesty than the one Sunday morning usually allows. To say the whole terrible thing to the God who wrote the words down for us to say. To bring him the fury and keep holding on. And to trust, not that the pain will be quickly explained, but that the One who authored our complaints is strong enough, and near enough, and kind enough, to hear them.

scriptureStudy.note: How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever? The psalm opens with four raw accusations and no apology, and God put it in the songbook, which means this is not the failure of worship but a sanctioned form of it.

My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? The cry Jesus takes onto his own lips from the cross begins here, in a lament, which means the sinless Son of God prayed the language of protest and did not sin in praying it.

You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness. This lament never turns to the light, ending in the dark, and God left it in Scripture anyway, a promise that even the prayer that finds no resolution is still received.

Why have you forgotten me? Why do I go mourning? and yet, Hope in God, for I shall again praise him. The psalm shows the turn happening in real time, the complaint and the self-summons to hope held in the same breath.

Remember my affliction, the wormwood and the gall. But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope. The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases. The turn in Lamentations comes not by denying the affliction but by calling something else to mind alongside it, hope remembered inside the grief, not instead of it.

O Lord, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? A prophet opens his book by accusing God of not listening, and the book is Scripture, further proof that the honest protest is not the enemy of faith but a form God honors.

My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. In Gethsemane Jesus does not perform a serene faith over his anguish but names the sorrow at its full weight, showing that lament is not beneath the Son of God but native to him.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the scholarship the church too rarely lets teach it here, and test it against Scripture rather than swallowing it whole. The Old Testament scholar Walter Brueggemann argued influentially that the Psalms move through a shape of orientation, disorientation, and new orientation, and that the modern church, by singing almost only the psalms of orientation and praise, has effectively censored the psalms of disorientation, the laments, from its worship, and in doing so has left its people with no sanctioned language for their pain. A group should weigh this carefully and honestly, noticing how exactly it names the Sunday-morning dishonesty the session describes, and asking what it has cost a congregation to lose two-thirds of its own inheritance of prayer. The finding is worth taking seriously as a diagnosis, and worth bringing under Scripture rather than treating as the last word, because the cure Brueggemann points toward is not novel therapy but the recovery of the Bible's own neglected songs. Set this beside the pastoral witness of Nicholas Wolterstorff, whose Lament for a Son, written after his twenty-five-year-old son died in a climbing accident in 1983, refuses every consolation that would make the death smaller and insists that the right response to a great loss is not to explain it but to grieve it fully before God. A group should sit with his hard sentence, that faith is not the absence of the wound but the trust that keeps holding on inside it. Then press the harder theological question this session most needs. If a third of the Psalms are laments, then a church that cannot lament is not more faithful than the Bible but less, and has confused emotional composure with spiritual maturity. Ask what it would mean for a congregation, and for the people in this room, to recover lament as a normal and honored part of the life of faith, so that the grieving are not made to feel like failures and the whole church learns again to say the true thing to God. The aim is not to make anyone morbid, but to give sorrow its scriptural voice back, so that trust is reached through honesty rather than around it.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in your group lost a pregnancy several months ago and has been, by every outward sign, doing beautifully, serving, smiling, quick to say that God is good and that she is at peace. When the session names the forced brightness that hides a wound, she goes quiet, and then admits, carefully, that she has not actually cried since it happened, because she was afraid that grieving would mean she did not trust God. Here is the work for the leader, and it must be tender and unhurried. Do not treat her peace as fake, because some of it may be real, and do not pull the scab off in front of the room. But gently give her back what the church took from her, the permission to grieve without it counting against her faith. Show her that the psalmists wept and accused and asked why and were not rebuked for it, that Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb knowing he would raise him, that her tears would not be a failure of trust but an act of it, bringing the real loss to the real God. Do not push her to break down on the spot. Offer instead a lament psalm to pray this week and a private conversation if she wants one, and let her discover, in her own time, that the God she is protecting can be trusted with the grief she has been hiding from him. Her composure is not the goal. Her honesty with God is.

memoryVerse.text: The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.

sessions.title: A God Who Does Not Explain, but Comes
sessions.aim: To see that God's final response to suffering is not an argument but a participation, that at the cross God enters the godforsakenness of the world rather than accounting for it from a safe distance, and to refuse both the deism that keeps God untouched above pain and the despair that reads pain as proof of his absence.
sessions.summary: Bell says that for most of his years as an atheist the cross meant nothing to him, and then one day it meant everything, and the hinge was suffering. He had assumed that if there were a God, he would be the kind of being who stayed above the mess, serene, untouched, explaining the world's agony from a safe distance or ignoring it altogether. The Christian claim turned out to be stranger than his atheism had prepared him for. The real question this session asks is where God was when it hurt, and Christianity's answer is not a theory but a place. He was on a cross, forsaken, crying out the opening line of a lament psalm, entering the very godforsakenness that the problem of pain is made of. The theologian Jurgen Moltmann, who came to faith as a prisoner of war after the Second World War, wrote a book called The Crucified God, arguing that God is not the impassive spectator of human suffering but the one who took it into his own being at Golgotha, so that there is no depth of human abandonment where God has not already been. Bell takes the strong case for the objection, that a God who suffers is a weak God, that the philosophers were right to want him untouchable and complete. He grants the instinct behind it. But a God who cannot suffer cannot love, because love that risks nothing and feels nothing is not love, and the cross reveals a God whose power is precisely his willingness to be wounded. Then the turn. This does not explain suffering. It does something better and harder. It means that when you go down into the dark, you do not go where God has never been. He has been there first, and he is there still, and the marks are on his hands.

keyScripture.why: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani? which means, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? showing God himself entering the depth of human godforsakenness and praying the language of lament from inside it, so that no abandonment is beyond the reach of a God who has already been there.

discussion.q: Bell says he once assumed that if God existed he would stay above the mess, serene and untouched. What have you assumed God does with human suffering, and where did that picture come from?
discussion.behind: Open by surfacing the operating picture, because most people carry an unexamined one. Many quietly assume a distant, unbothered God, either explaining pain from above or ignoring it. Help the room name the God they actually imagine when they hurt, before the session offers the God the cross reveals, because the gap between the two is where the whole session lives.

discussion.q: Christianity's answer to where God was when it hurt is not a theory but a place, a cross. What changes when the answer to your suffering is not an explanation but a God who entered it?
discussion.behind: Get to the heart of the session's claim. The gospel does not finally answer the problem of pain with an argument, it answers it with a person who bore it. Help the room feel the difference between a God who explains suffering from a distance and a God who climbs into it, and why the second, though it solves less intellectually, comforts more deeply. Do not let it stay abstract.

discussion.q: Jesus cried out My God, my God, why have you forsaken me, the opening line of a lament psalm, from the cross. What does it mean to you that God himself has prayed the prayer of the forsaken?
discussion.behind: Press on the astonishing specificity. The Son of God does not float serenely through his death, he enters abandonment and prays the language of protest we studied last week. Help the room see that there is no place of godforsakenness they can reach that God in Christ has not already entered, and that the cry from the cross means their darkest prayer has already been prayed by God himself.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that a God who suffers is a weak God, that the philosophers wanted him untouchable. What is true in wanting a strong God, and why does Bell say a God who cannot suffer cannot love?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The longing for a strong, stable God is not wrong, and there is real philosophical weight behind the idea that God is complete and unchanging. But press the deeper point, that love by its nature is vulnerable, that a being who risks and feels nothing cannot love, and that the cross reveals a strength that includes the willingness to be wounded. Help the room hold God's power and God's woundedness together rather than trading one for the other.

discussion.q: Bell says this does not explain suffering but does something harder, it means you never go into the dark where God has not been first. Where in your own pain would it change things to know God had been there before you?
discussion.behind: Move toward the personal and go first if the room is slow. This is the pastoral payload of the session, that the sufferer is not alone in a place God avoids but accompanied in a place God has already entered. Invite people to name the specific dark they have walked or are walking, and to consider that the marks on Christ's hands mean he met them there. End in weight and presence, not tidy resolution.

objections.objection: A God who suffers and cries out in abandonment is just a weak, human-sized God. The whole point of God is that he is above all that, complete and unchanging, and a wounded God is no help to anyone because he needs saving as much as we do.
objections.response: Grant the instinct, because it is ancient and serious and not foolish. The philosophers who insisted God must be complete, unchanging, and beyond suffering were guarding something real, that God is not a bigger version of us, buffeted and needy, and a god who was merely a cosmic sufferer with no power to save would indeed be no gospel. Hold that. But the cross does not show us a weak God overwhelmed by pain against his will. It shows us the God of all power freely choosing to enter the one place his creatures most needed him, the depth of abandonment, and to do it without ceasing to be God. That is not weakness. It is the highest strength there is, because it is the strength that can afford to be wounded. And here is the point the objection cannot answer, a God who cannot suffer cannot love, because love that feels nothing and risks nothing and cannot be moved is not love at all, it is indifference with good manners. The God who stayed safely above the mess would be philosophically tidy and finally useless in a hospital room. The God of the cross is the one who can meet you there, because he has bled there.

objections.objection: Even if God suffered on the cross, that was one afternoon two thousand years ago. It does nothing about my suffering now, today, in this body, in this loss. A historical crucifixion is not company in my actual pain.
objections.response: Take the honesty seriously, because the distance in it is real and felt, and no one should be told a doctrine when they need a presence. But the cross is not merely a past event the Christian admires from a distance. It is the revelation of who God permanently is, the God whose love takes the shape of entering rather than avoiding, and the same God who entered abandonment at Golgotha is, by his Spirit, present in the hospital room now, not as a memory but as a companion. When Scripture says the Lord is near to the brokenhearted, it is not speaking of a God who was once briefly near long ago. It is describing his settled character, proved at the cross and enacted in every dark place since. This does not remove your pain, and the study will not pretend it does. What it changes is the deepest thing, whether you suffer alone in a place God avoids, or accompanied in a place God has already entered and enters still. The marks on his hands are not a museum piece. They are the permanent sign that he does not stay away.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: In the darkest place your suffering has taken you, did you experience God as absent from it or present in it, and how would the cross reread that memory?
sessions.practice: This week, take the specific dark you have known, the loss or the fear or the abandonment, and sit with the cross beside it, deliberately, in prayer. Do not try to explain your suffering and do not ask the cross to explain it either. Simply hold the two together and say to God that he has been in this place before you, that the cry of the forsaken was his cry too, and ask him to make his presence in your dark as real as his absence has sometimes felt. Write down whether holding your pain next to the cross changed anything about how alone the pain felt.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, we expected a God who stayed above our suffering, safe and serene and explaining our pain from a distance, and instead you came down into it and let it close over your head. You cried out the prayer of the forsaken so that no forsaken person would ever again be alone in the dark. Forgive us for wanting a God too strong to be wounded, when the wounds are the very proof of how you love. Where we have felt abandoned, teach us that you were there before us and are there still. Make the marks on your hands more real to us than the absence we have feared. And for everyone in this room carrying a grief too heavy to name, come, not with an answer, but with yourself, the God who bled. Amen.
reflection: What picture of God do I actually carry into my suffering, the untouched spectator or the God who entered the dark, and how would the cross correct it?
Have I wanted a God too strong to be wounded, and what would it mean to trust the strength that chose the wounds instead?
Where have I felt most abandoned, and what would change if I believed God had already been in that exact place before me?
sessions.teaching: Bell says that for most of the years he did not believe, the cross meant nothing to him. It was a piece of religious furniture, a symbol other people found moving, an execution he could not see the point of. And then one day it meant everything, and the hinge on which that turned was suffering. Because here is what his atheism had quietly assumed about God, in the years he was arguing against him. He assumed that if there were a God at all, he would be the kind of being who stayed above the mess. Serene. Complete. Untouched. A God who ran the universe from a safe distance, either explaining its agony with some plan too high for us to see, or, more likely, simply not bothered by it, too far above the wreckage to feel it. And on that assumption the problem of pain really is unanswerable, because a God who could stop your child's suffering and merely watches from his untroubled height is a monster, and Bell wanted no part of him. What broke the assumption was discovering that the Christian claim about God was stranger, and harder, than anything his unbelief had prepared him for. So the real question this session puts is the oldest and most personal question a sufferer ever asks. Where was God when it hurt. Not in the abstract, but where was he when the phone rang, when the room went silent, when the prayer came back empty. And Christianity's answer to that question is not a theory. It is not a syllogism or a plan or a reason. It is a place. He was on a cross. He was in the dark at noon, nails through his hands, crying out the opening line of a lament psalm, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, entering the very godforsakenness that the whole problem of pain is made of. The theologian Jurgen Moltmann is worth knowing here, because he did not learn this in a library. He learned it as a young German soldier taken prisoner at the end of the Second World War, in the camps, as the full horror of what his nation had done became known to him and his own hope collapsed, and it was there, reading the Gospels, that he found he could not bear a God who had not suffered, and could just barely begin to live again because of a God who had. Years later he wrote a book called The Crucified God, and its argument is the center of this session. God, Moltmann said, is not the impassive spectator of the world's agony. At the cross God took human suffering into his own being, into the very life of the Trinity, so that there is no depth of human abandonment where God has not already been. Moltmann tells the story, from Elie Wiesel's memoir of the camps, of a child left hanging on the gallows while the prisoners were forced to watch, and a man behind him asking, where is God now, and Moltmann's answer, the whole answer of the cross, is that God was there, hanging on the gallows, entering that death from the inside. Take the strong case against this, because it has a long and serious pedigree and I do not want to be glib about it. The philosophers, going back to the Greeks and running deep into Christian theology, insisted that God must be impassible, incapable of suffering, because suffering implies need, change, incompleteness, and God is complete. A God who suffers, the objection runs, is a weak God, a human-sized God, and a weak God is no gospel because he needs rescuing as badly as we do. There is a real truth being guarded there, that God is not just a bigger, sadder version of us. Grant it. But the cross does not show us a God overwhelmed by suffering against his will. It shows us the God of all power freely choosing to enter the one place his creatures most needed him to be, and to enter it without ceasing for one moment to be God. And it exposes what the philosophers' tidy God could never do. Because a God who cannot suffer cannot love. Love that risks nothing, feels nothing, can be moved by nothing, is not love, it is indifference in a nicer suit. The strength the objection wants, the untouchable completeness, turns out to be the very thing that would make God unable to do the one thing the cross reveals he does. He loves. And love, real love, is always willing to be wounded. So here is the turn, and it is the whole session, and I have to say clearly what it is and what it is not. This does not explain suffering. If you came to this study hoping the cross would finally give you the reason your grief has been demanding, I have to tell you honestly that it does not. God still does not hand Job the wager. What the cross does is harder and, in the hospital room, better. It means that when you go down into the dark, you do not go where God has never been. He has been there first. He went down into abandonment ahead of you and came out the other side, and by his Spirit he is in the dark with you now, not as a memory of an execution long ago but as the permanent character of a God who does not stay away. I know the difference this makes because I have needed it, not as an argument but as company. There is a kind of suffering that no explanation would touch even if you had one, where the only thing that helps is that you are not alone in it. And the gospel's deepest word to the sufferer is not here is why. It is I am here. The marks are on his hands. He has been where you are. And he did not leave.

scriptureStudy.note: He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief. Centuries before the cross, the servant of the Lord is described not as a stranger to suffering but as its intimate, one who knows grief from the inside, which is who God turned out to be.

My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? God the Son enters real abandonment and prays the language of lament from within it, so that the cry of the forsaken has already been God's own cry, and no one prays it alone.
Jesus wept. At the tomb of his friend, moments before raising him, Jesus grieves, which means God does not stand above our sorrow explaining it but enters it and cries, even when he knows the ending.

We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are. The God we come to in suffering is not a stranger to it but one who has felt it from the inside and can sympathize because he has been there.

Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. Scripture is unembarrassed to say that the incarnate Son learned obedience through suffering, entering the human experience of pain so fully that it formed him, which no distant, untouched God could do.

Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. The movement of God is downward, from the height the philosophers guarded into the lowest place, and Scripture calls that descent not weakness but the very glory of God.

In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them. Long before the cross, God is described as afflicted in his people's affliction, present in their suffering rather than aloof from it, the character the cross would finally reveal in full.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the theological debate this session touches, because the question of whether God can suffer is one of the oldest and most consequential in Christian thought, and a group should handle it with care rather than settling it in a sentence. The classical tradition, drawing on Greek philosophy and running through Augustine and Aquinas, held to divine impassibility, the conviction that God in his divine nature cannot suffer or change, and this was not carelessness but an attempt to guard God's perfection and freedom, to keep him from being a needy, buffeted being at the mercy of the world. Twentieth-century theologians, Jurgen Moltmann chief among them in The Crucified God, published in German in 1972, challenged this, arguing that the cross reveals a God who genuinely enters suffering, and that a God who cannot suffer cannot love. A group should weigh both sides honestly rather than assuming the modern view simply wins, because the classical tradition was protecting something real, that God is not overwhelmed by evil, and the modern correction is naming something equally real, that the cross shows God entering pain rather than avoiding it. The most careful path holds both, that God does not suffer as we do, helplessly and against his will, and yet freely takes suffering into himself in Christ out of love. Set this beside Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who wrote from a Nazi prison, in the months before his execution in 1945, that only a suffering God can help, a line worth sitting with because it comes not from a comfortable study but from a cell. Then bring the whole discussion under Scripture rather than leaving it in philosophy, because the Bible's testimony is not a theory of impassibility or passibility but a narrative, a God who weeps at a tomb, who is afflicted in his people's affliction, who cries out forsaken from a cross. The aim is not to win a technical debate but to let a suffering group discover that the God they come to is not a stranger to their pain, and to hold the mystery, that he is both strong enough to save and near enough to weep, without collapsing either half.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group has been circling the edges of faith for months, honest and searching, and he says plainly that the suffering he has seen, a friend's long death from cancer, is the main thing keeping him from believing, that he cannot worship a God who would allow it. He is not being provocative. He is being truthful, and he is exactly the skeptic this study writes toward. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor his objection before it answers it. Do not rush to defend God, and do not treat his unbelief as a problem to be fixed in one evening. Grant first that his objection is serious and that a God who merely watched his friend die from an untroubled distance would deserve the rejection. Then, gently, offer him not an argument but the strange fact at the center of the faith, that the God he is rejecting is not the untouched spectator he imagines, but the one who entered suffering himself and cried out forsaken. Show him that Christianity does not answer his friend's death with a reason but with a God who has been in the grave. Do not press for a decision, because the endings of this study leave weight rather than demand a verdict. Let him leave able to disagree and still thinking, and let the cross do its slow work, so that even if he walks out still unconvinced, he walks out no longer able to say that believing is the same as pretending the suffering does not matter. It matters most of all to the God at the center of it.

memoryVerse.text: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.

sessions.title: The Thorn That Was Not Removed
sessions.aim: To take seriously the slow work that suffering can do, the endurance and character and hope Paul names, without ever flattening it into a formula that makes pain a tidy means to a good end, and to sit honestly with the prayer God answered by not removing the thorn.
sessions.summary: Bell says the most misused verse in the Bible in a hospital room is Romans 8:28, that God works all things together for good, not because it is untrue but because of how fast we say it and to whom. In the mouth of a sufferer, wrestled toward over years, it is hard-won faith. In the mouth of a bystander, offered in the first raw week, it is a lid slapped on a grief. The real question is what suffering actually does, and whether Scripture lets us say anything honest about it without turning pain into a machine that manufactures growth. Paul says something careful and strange. Suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope. It is a real sequence, but notice it is not a promise that every pain pays off on a schedule, and notice who is saying it, a man who was beaten, shipwrecked, imprisoned, and left with a thorn in the flesh he begged God three times to remove. God said no. Not this will make sense later, not here is why, just my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. Bell takes the strong case against all of this, the objection that talk of suffering producing character is obscene when you are standing over a child's grave, that some pain produces nothing but ruin. He grants it fully, because it is often true and the formula has done real harm. But there is a difference between saying suffering produces good, which is a lie, and saying God can bring good out of suffering, which is the testimony of people who have been through it and come out holding onto him. Then the turn. The deepest gift is not the thorn removed but the presence given in its place, not the pain explained but grace proved sufficient in it, and a strength that shows up precisely where you are weakest and admits it.

keyScripture.why: But he said to me, My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness, recording God's answer to Paul's threefold prayer for relief, an answer that does not remove the thorn or explain it but promises a sufficient grace and a power perfected in the very place of weakness.

discussion.q: Bell says Romans 8:28 is true but often misused, hard-won faith in a sufferer's mouth and a lid slapped on grief in a bystander's. Have you been on either end of that verse, and how did it land?
discussion.behind: Open on the lived experience of a much-quoted verse. Almost everyone has either been handed this verse too fast or handed it to someone else. The point is not that the verse is false, it is deeply true, but that the same words are faith when won and cruelty when imposed. Help the room feel the difference timing and ownership make, without dismissing the verse itself.

discussion.q: Paul says suffering produces endurance, endurance character, character hope, but he says it as a man with a thorn God would not remove. Why does it matter that the one making this claim was himself denied relief?
discussion.behind: Get under the credibility of the claim. The sequence in Romans 5 could sound like a cheap formula until you notice who wrote it, a man well acquainted with unrelieved pain. Help the room see that Paul is not theorizing from comfort but testifying from the ash heap, which is the only place such a claim can be made without becoming an insult. The messenger authenticates the message.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that talk of suffering producing character is obscene at a child's grave, that some pain produces only ruin. What is true in that, and how is it different from saying God can bring good out of suffering?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves with real care, because this is where the formula does its harm. Grant fully that suffering does not automatically produce anything good, that plenty of it destroys, and that saying otherwise over a fresh grave is cruelty. Then draw the careful line, the difference between suffering produces good, which is false, and God can bring good out of suffering, which is testimony. Protect the grieving in the room from the formula while keeping the hope honest.

discussion.q: God answered Paul's prayer for relief not by removing the thorn but by promising sufficient grace and power made perfect in weakness. Have you ever received a no that came with grace instead of an explanation?
discussion.behind: Move toward the personal center. Many in the room have prayed for a thing to be taken away and watched it stay. Help them consider that God's no to Paul was not abandonment but a different kind of yes, grace in the thing rather than rescue from it. Do not force a triumphant reading, because for some the thorn is still fresh and the grace not yet felt. Let them sit with the honest question.

discussion.q: Bell says the deepest gift is not the thorn removed but the presence given in its place, and a strength that shows up where you are weakest. Where are you still asking God to remove a thorn, and what would it mean to ask instead for grace sufficient in it?
discussion.behind: Close on the reframe, gently, and go first. This is a hard turn and it must not be rushed or imposed, because asking for grace in the thorn rather than removal of it is a costly prayer that cannot be demanded of someone still bleeding. Invite it as an offer, not a command. Let people name the thorn they keep begging God to take, and consider, if they are ready, the harder and deeper prayer underneath it. End in weight.

objections.objection: Telling people their suffering is producing character or growth is offensive when they are living through the worst thing that ever happened to them. Plenty of suffering just destroys people, and turning pain into a self-improvement program is a lie.
objections.response: Grant this fully and first, because it is largely true and the failure to grant it has wounded countless grieving people. Suffering does not automatically produce anything good. It often produces bitterness, breakdown, and ruin, and to stand over a fresh grave and talk about the character being built is not comfort, it is an obscenity, and Scripture never asks us to say such a thing. Hold that without flinching. But notice the exact line the objection blurs, because everything depends on it. There is a world of difference between saying suffering produces good, which is a formula and a lie, and saying God can bring good out of suffering, which is not a formula at all but the testimony of people who have walked through the dark and come out still holding on. Paul does not say the thorn was good. He says God's grace was sufficient in it. The claim is never that the pain is a blessing in disguise, which cheapens the pain and insults the sufferer. The claim is that God is able to redeem even what he did not send and would not call good, and that is not a program you impose on someone, it is a hope you can only discover from the inside, usually long after, and never on command.

objections.objection: If God could remove Paul's thorn and simply chose not to, then God is willing to let people suffer when he could stop it. That does not make God loving, it makes his refusal to help the whole problem all over again.
objections.response: Take the weight of this, because it is the problem of pain returning in a sharper, more personal form, and it deserves no evasion. God could have removed the thorn. He said no. And that no is genuinely hard, because it means God sometimes allows a suffering he has the power to end. Do not soften that. But look closely at what the no actually contained, because it was not silence and it was not indifference. God answered, and the answer was a promise of his own sufficient grace and a power perfected in the very place of Paul's weakness, which means the no was not the withholding of help but the giving of a different and deeper help than the one requested. Paul asked for the thorn gone. God gave Paul himself, present in the thorn, and Paul concluded, astonishingly, that he would rather have the weakness with the grace than the strength without it. This does not resolve the problem of why God permits any suffering, and the study will not pretend it does. What it shows is that God's no is not always abandonment, that sometimes the refusal to remove the pain is joined to a presence in the pain that the sufferer comes to treasure more than the rescue he first begged for.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the thorn you have asked God three times, or three hundred times, to remove, and could you begin to ask instead for grace sufficient to bear it, or is that prayer still too costly to pray?
sessions.practice: This week, take the thorn you keep asking God to remove and change one prayer. Do not stop asking for relief if you need to, but add the harder prayer alongside it, that his grace would prove sufficient in the thing while it remains, and that his strength would show up in your weakness rather than by ending it. Watch, through the week, for the grace that comes not as rescue but as enough, the strength that meets you in the weakness instead of taking it away. Write down whether asking for grace in the thorn, rather than only its removal, changed anything about how you carried it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have prayed for the thorn to be taken, again and again, and sometimes you have taken it and sometimes you have said what you said to Paul, that your grace is enough and your strength is made perfect in our weakness. Forgive us the times we turned your servants' suffering into a formula, told the grieving their pain was making them better, and slapped a good verse over a wound that needed only our silence and our tears. Teach us the difference between the lie that suffering produces good and the hope that you can bring good out of suffering. Where the thorn remains, give us grace sufficient to bear it, and a strength that meets us in the weakness rather than around it. And where a burden has grown too heavy, send us people to help carry it, and make us those people for someone else. Amen.
reflection: Where have I turned suffering into a formula, telling myself or others that pain automatically produces growth, and how has that lie cost me honesty?
Have I only ever asked God to remove my thorn, or have I been willing to ask for grace sufficient to bear it, and what does my reluctance reveal?
What would it mean to believe that God's strength is made perfect in my weakness, rather than by finally making me strong enough to need no grace?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the most misused verse in the Bible in a hospital room is Romans 8:28, that God works all things together for good for those who love him. And he is careful, because the verse is not false. It is gloriously true, and it has held up more grieving saints than anyone could count. The problem is not the verse. The problem is how fast we say it, and to whom. In the mouth of a sufferer who has fought her way toward it over years of dark, it is one of the hardest-won and most precious sentences in all of Scripture. In the mouth of a bystander, tossed off in the first raw week of someone else's grief, the same words become a lid slapped down on a wound that was still trying to breathe. Same verse. One is faith. The other is a way of making the sufferer's pain more manageable for the person who cannot stand to sit in it. So the real question of this session is a careful one. What does suffering actually do, and can we say anything honest about it at all without turning pain into a machine that manufactures growth on a schedule. Because there is a version of Christian teaching that does exactly that, that treats every hardship as an investment guaranteed to pay a spiritual dividend, and that version is not only false, it is cruel, and it has driven wounded people out of the church for good reason. Now watch how carefully Paul actually speaks, because he is not careless the way we are. In Romans 5 he writes that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame. It is a real sequence, and I do not want to explain it away. But notice two things about it. First, it is not a promise that every pain pays off on a timetable you can hold God to, it is a description of what God can grow in a life surrendered to him, not a formula the sufferer can invoke to make the ache productive. And second, notice who is saying it. This is not a comfortable man theorizing about other people's pain. This is Paul, who was beaten with rods, whipped near to death five times, shipwrecked, stoned and left for dead, imprisoned for years, and who carried, on top of all of it, something he called a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass him, some affliction we are never told the name of, and it does not matter that we are not told, because the point is that it did not lift. He begged God to take it away. Three times, he says, which in the biblical way of speaking means he prayed it to the floor, prayed it until there was nothing left to pray. And God's answer is one of the most important sentences in the Bible for anyone who has ever prayed for relief that did not come. God did not say, this will make sense later. God did not say, here is the reason. God did not even say yes. God said, my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. Take the strong case against everything I have just said, because it needs to be stated at full strength and I have stood near enough graves to feel it. The objection is that all this talk of suffering producing endurance and character is not just unhelpful but obscene when you are standing over the small coffin of a child, that there are sufferings which produce nothing at all except ruin, which break people and do not build them, which leave nothing redemptive in their wake no matter how long you wait. Grant it. Grant all of it, because it is often simply true, and the refusal to grant it is exactly what has made the formula so hateful. Suffering does not automatically produce good. It frequently produces bitterness and breakdown, and to tell a devastated parent that their loss is building their character is to commit a sin against them with a Bible verse. But here is the line the objection blurs, and the whole session hangs on it. There is a difference, an enormous one, between saying suffering produces good, and saying God can bring good out of suffering. The first is a formula, and it is a lie. The second is not a formula at all.
