It is the testimony of people who have gone down into the worst of it and come out the far side still holding on to God, and it can only ever be said from the inside, in the past tense, by the person who suffered, and never imposed from the outside on someone still bleeding. Paul never says the thorn was good. He says God's grace was sufficient in it. That is the whole difference. So here is the turn, and it is where I have had to live myself, because I have prayed the three-times prayer and gotten the answer Paul got. The deepest gift God gives the sufferer is very often not the thorn removed. It is the presence given in the thorn's place. Not the pain explained, which he mostly does not do, but grace proved sufficient in the middle of it, and a strange strength that shows up precisely where you are weakest and stops pretending to be strong. Paul ends up in a place that sounds like madness until you have been there. He says he will boast in his weaknesses, that he is content with them, because when he is weak, then he is strong, because the weakness is the very place the grace shows up. That is not the power of positive thinking and it is not the thorn made pretty. It is a man who asked for rescue, received presence instead, and discovered that the presence was worth more than the rescue would have been. Most of us will spend years asking God to remove the thorn. The harder, deeper, and finally better prayer, the one Paul was driven to, is to ask for grace sufficient to bear it, and to find that the grace was there all along, made perfect in exactly the weakness we kept begging him to take away.

scriptureStudy.note: Suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame. The sequence is real but not a formula, a description of what God grows in a surrendered life, spoken by a man well acquainted with unrelieved pain.

A thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me. Scripture never names the thorn, and the silence is a mercy, because it lets every sufferer with an unlifted affliction find themselves in Paul's unhealed wound.

Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this. But he said to me, My grace is sufficient for you. God answers a prayer for relief not with removal or explanation but with sufficient grace, the deepest evidence that a no from God is not the same as abandonment.

For those who love God all things work together for good. True and precious when won by a sufferer, cruel when slapped over a fresh grief by a bystander, the verse promises not that suffering is good but that God can weave good even from what he did not send.

Count it all joy when you meet trials, for the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. James, like Paul, ties trial to endurance, but the joy is counted, chosen and worked toward, not felt automatically, and it is aimed at maturity, not at pretending the trial is painless.

Though now for a little while you have been grieved by various trials, the tested genuineness of your faith is more precious than gold. Peter grants the grief its full weight, now and real, before speaking of what the testing refines, refusing to rush past the sorrow to the outcome.

Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. Paul holds the wasting and the renewing together in one sentence, neither denying the decay nor letting it be the last word, which is the honest shape of hope in suffering.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the pastoral theology this session most needs, because the ground between denying that suffering can form us and claiming that it automatically improves us is narrow, and a group can fall off either side. Timothy Keller, in Walking with God through Pain and Suffering, published in 2013, surveys the ways different cultures and philosophies have tried to make sense of pain and argues that the Christian account is distinct in refusing both to minimize suffering as illusion and to treat it as meaningless, holding instead that God can use it without our ever being required to call it good. A group should weigh this against the real danger Keller himself warns of, the prosperity teaching that promises suffering will always be brief and productive if you have enough faith, a teaching this study names plainly as false and cruel. Set that beside the older tradition, running through figures like the Puritans and recovered in our time, that spoke of affliction as a school, while being careful to notice how easily that language curdles into the formula when it is spoken over someone else's grief rather than out of one's own. Then take up the secular research honestly and bring it under Scripture rather than beside it. Psychologists have described what they call post-traumatic growth, the finding that some people emerge from severe suffering with deepened relationships, priorities, and strength, and a group should grant what is true in it, that suffering is not always merely destructive, while naming what it cannot see, that growth is never guaranteed, that plenty of trauma produces only wreckage, and that the research describes a possibility, not a promise, and certainly not a comfort to offer the freshly bereaved. The Christian claim is deeper and more careful than the finding, that God can bring good out of what he did not send, on a timeline he does not disclose, by a grace the sufferer receives rather than manufactures. The aim of this session is to let a hurting group hold, in one hand, the honesty that some pain produces nothing but ruin, and in the other, the hope that God is able to redeem even this, without ever collapsing the second into the formula that has done so much harm.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in your group lives with chronic pain that no treatment has relieved, and she has heard, for years, from well-meaning believers, that God must be building something in her, that there is a purpose, that she will understand one day. She is exhausted by it, and when the session begins she is braced for more of the same. Here is the work for the leader, and it must refuse the formula before it offers anything else. Do not tell her what her suffering is producing, because that is exactly the cruelty she has endured, and you are not standing in her body. Grant plainly that her pain may not produce anything she can point to, that the people who kept explaining it to her were wrong to, and that God has not told her the reason. Then, carefully and without imposing it, offer her the one thing the formula never did, the possibility that God's answer to her, as to Paul, might not be removal or explanation but a grace sufficient to bear it and a presence in the pain itself. Do not require her to feel that grace on cue, and do not turn the sufficient grace into a new formula. Let her hear that Paul, too, was denied relief, that his thorn stayed, and that he was not told why either, so that she is not alone in the unanswered prayer. The gift you can give her is not another explanation but the end of the demand that she produce one, and the company of a God, and a group, willing to stay in the pain with her rather than accounting for it.

memoryVerse.text: But he said to me, My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.

sessions.title: Every Tear, and Whose Hand Wipes It
sessions.aim: To place all suffering under the promise of the new creation, where every tear is wiped away by the hand of God himself, to name present suffering as penultimate rather than final, and to refuse both the sentimentality that skips to the ending and the despair that cannot believe there is one.
sessions.summary: Bell says the two cheapest things you can do with the Christian hope are to grab it too early and to give it up entirely, and grief is tempted toward both. The real question this session asks is whether the suffering we have spent five weeks refusing to explain gets the last word, and the answer at the heart of the faith is no, but not a no that arrives cheaply. Revelation ends not with souls escaping to a disembodied heaven but with heaven coming down, a new creation, God dwelling with his people, and a single sentence that has carried more grief than perhaps any other in Scripture. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away. Notice whose hand does the wiping. Not an angel, not a servant, God himself, bending down to the face of every sufferer. Bell takes the strong case for the skeptic, that this is wishful thinking, pie in the sky, a comfort invented precisely because the world is unbearable without it. He grants the suspicion its full weight, because a hope that cannot survive being doubted is not worth having. But the Christian hope is not grounded in how much we need it. It is grounded in an empty tomb, in a resurrection claimed as an event and not a metaphor, the first piece of the new creation breaking into the old. Then the turn, and the word Bonhoeffer gave us, penultimate. Present suffering is not nothing, and this study has refused every attempt to make it nothing. But it is not ultimate. It is real, and it is the next-to-last word, and there is a last word coming, spoken by the God who bends down himself to dry the face of everyone who ever wept. Not yet. But surely. And the not yet is why we still weep, and the surely is why we do not weep as those who have no hope.

keyScripture.why: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away, naming the last word over all suffering, spoken by the hand of God himself bending to every grieving face, and making present pain penultimate rather than final.

discussion.q: Bell says the two cheapest things you can do with Christian hope are to grab it too early and to give it up entirely. Which of those are you more tempted toward in your suffering, and why?
discussion.behind: Open by naming the two failures of hope, because most people lean toward one. Grabbing it early skips the grief and rushes to the ending, which is sentimentality. Giving it up abandons the ending altogether, which is despair. Help the room locate their own tilt honestly, and see that both are ways of not holding the hard middle, where the pain is real and the hope is real at the same time.

discussion.q: Revelation ends not with escape to a disembodied heaven but with heaven coming down and God dwelling with his people. What changes when the Christian hope is not leaving this world but its healing?
discussion.behind: Correct the common picture, gently. Many imagine the hope as souls floating off to a cloud, and the actual biblical hope is far more solid and world-affirming, a new creation where God dwells with embodied people. Help the room feel that this hope honors the goodness of the world and the reality of the body, and takes their present grief seriously precisely because the thing lost will be restored, not discarded.

discussion.q: The verse says God himself, not an angel, will wipe away every tear from their eyes. What does it mean to you that the hand that dries your face at the end is God's own?
discussion.behind: Press on the tenderness and the specificity. The comfort is not a general improvement of conditions but an intimate act, God bending to each face. Help the room feel that this is personal, that the God who entered suffering at the cross is the same God who kneels at the end to dry each individual tear. Connect it back to session three, the God who wept now the God who wipes tears away.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that this hope is wishful thinking, invented because the world is unbearable without it. What is true in that suspicion, and why does Bell say the hope rests on an empty tomb rather than on our need for it?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves for the skeptic in the room. Grant that the suspicion is fair, that a comfort could be invented precisely because it is needed, and that a hope afraid of that question is weak. Then show the ground Christianity actually claims, not our need but a resurrection asserted as an event, the first piece of the new creation. Help the room see that the hope stands or falls not on how badly we want it but on whether the tomb was empty.

discussion.q: Bell says present suffering is penultimate, the next-to-last word, real but not ultimate. How would it change the way you carry your current pain to hold it as real and as not the final word at the same time?
discussion.behind: Close on the central reframe and let it land with weight rather than resolution. Penultimate holds both truths the whole study has fought for, that the suffering is real and must not be minimized, and that it is not final and will not have the last word. Help the room carry both at once, the not yet that lets them still weep and the surely that keeps them from weeping as those without hope. End the study here, in weight and in hope, not in a tidy bow.

objections.objection: The promise that God will wipe away every tear is obviously wishful thinking. Human beings invented heaven because life is unbearable without believing there is something better afterward. It is a comfort we made up precisely because we needed it.
objections.response: Grant the suspicion its full force, because it is honest and a hope too fragile to face it is not worth holding. It is true that a comfort can be invented because it is needed, that the very desperation of our situation could produce the wish, and Christianity gains nothing by pretending that objection is stupid. Hold it. But notice that the fact we need something does not by itself make it false, hunger does not prove there is no bread, and thirst is not evidence against water. The real question is not whether we want the hope but whether it is true, and Christianity does not finally rest its case on human need. It rests it on a claim about an event, that a man was dead and then was not, that the tomb was empty, that the resurrection happened in history as the first piece of the new creation breaking into the old. You can dispute that claim, and serious people do, but it is a claim about something that either occurred or did not, not a wish dressed up as a fact. The Christian does not believe in the new creation because the world is unbearable without it. He believes in it because he believes a grave came open on a Sunday morning, and everything else follows from whether that is true.

objections.objection: A future where every tear is wiped away does nothing about the tears right now. Promising people a happy ending someday is just a way of getting them to accept unbearable suffering in the present instead of doing something about it.
objections.response: Take the danger seriously, because it is real and the church has sometimes deserved the charge. A hope in the future can be misused to excuse indifference in the present, to tell the suffering to wait for heaven instead of meeting their pain now, and that misuse is a genuine sin, not a strength of the faith. Grant it. But the biblical hope, rightly held, does the opposite of numbing action, because the God who promises to wipe away every tear at the end is the same God who entered suffering at the cross in the middle, and who commands his people to weep with those who weep and to bind up the broken now. The new creation is not an excuse to ignore present pain, it is the guarantee that present pain matters so much that God himself will finally undo it, which is precisely why we take it seriously in the meantime rather than shrugging. And notice what the hope actually changes for the sufferer. It does not remove the tears now, and this study has insisted on that for five weeks. It changes whether the tears are the last word. The not yet is exactly why we still grieve, honestly and fully. The surely is why we do not grieve as those who have no hope. Both, at once, and neither one canceling the other.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you picture God himself bending down to wipe the tears from your face, and from the face of the person you have grieved most, what rises in you, and is it hope, or is it a hope you are afraid to let yourself feel?
sessions.practice: This week, hold your present grief and the promise of Revelation 21 together, deliberately, without letting either cancel the other. Name the tear you are still crying, honestly, refusing to skip to the ending. And then say, over that same grief, that it is real but not final, penultimate and not ultimate, and that the hand which will wipe it away is God's own. Do not force the feeling of hope. Just hold the two truths in the same hand, the not yet and the surely. Write down what it does to your grief to hold it as real and as not the last word at the same time.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have spent these weeks refusing to explain away the suffering, and we will not explain it away now, because it is real and you know it is real, you who wept at a grave. But we will not give the pain the last word either, because you have promised a last word of your own. You will wipe away every tear from every eye, with your own hand, and death will be no more, and mourning and crying and pain will be gone, and the former things will have passed away. We believe it not because we need it, though we do, but because the tomb was empty on a Sunday morning. Teach us to hold our grief as penultimate, real and not final. Let the not yet keep us honest and the surely keep us from despair. And for anyone in this room whose pain has grown too heavy to carry, let this be the day they reach for help and are not ashamed, and let us be the hands you send. Come, Lord Jesus, and until you do, keep us. Amen.
reflection: Am I more tempted to grab the hope too early and skip my grief, or to give it up entirely and skip the hope, and what would it mean to hold both?
Does the promise that God himself will wipe away my tears feel real to me, or like a hope I am afraid to let myself believe, and why?
What would change in how I carry my present suffering if I truly held it as penultimate, real but not the final word over my life?
sessions.teaching: Bell says there are two cheap things a person can do with the Christian hope, and grief is tempted toward both of them, sometimes in the same hour. The first is to grab the hope too early, to reach past the grief and snatch the happy ending before you have let yourself feel the loss, which produces the sentimentality that makes so much Christian talk about heaven unbearable to a person actually in pain. The second is to give the hope up entirely, to conclude that the wound is the whole truth and there is no ending coming, which is despair. And the hard, narrow, honest place this study has been trying to stand for five weeks is exactly between them, where the suffering is fully real and the hope is fully real at the same time, and neither one is allowed to cancel the other. So the real question of this final session is the one the whole study has been moving toward. Does the suffering we have refused to explain get the last word. And the answer at the very center of the Christian faith is no, but it is not a no that arrives cheaply, and I will not let it arrive cheaply here. Look at how the Bible actually ends, because it is not what most people imagine. It does not end with souls escaping this ruined world for a disembodied heaven somewhere else, floating off to a cloud. It ends with heaven coming down. It ends with a new creation, a renewed heaven and earth, and God himself coming to dwell with his people, the whole ache of the world's exile from God finally over. And in the middle of that vision stands a single sentence that has been read at more gravesides and whispered over more deathbeds than perhaps any other in Scripture. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away. Sit with it slowly, because we say it so often we have stopped hearing it. Every tear. Not most. Not the ones that were justified. Every tear that has ever fallen, from every eye, accounted for and dried. And death itself, the last enemy, the thing behind so much of our grief, not managed or explained but abolished, no more. And notice, because this is the tenderest thing in the whole vision, whose hand does the wiping. It is not an angel dispatched for the task. It is not a servant. It is God himself, the text says, bending down to the face of every sufferer who ever lived, and wiping the tears away with his own hand. The God who wept at Lazarus's tomb in session three is the God who kneels here at the end to dry every face. Take the strong case against all of this, the skeptic's case, and take it seriously, because I made it myself for years and a hope that cannot survive the question is not worth having. The objection is that this is obviously wishful thinking. Human beings invented heaven, the argument goes, precisely because life is unbearable without believing there is something better on the other side, that the very desperation of our condition manufactured the comfort, and that the more beautiful and consoling the promise is, the more suspicious we should be that we made it up to soothe ourselves. Grant the weight of it. It is true that a comfort can be invented because it is needed. But here is what the objection quietly assumes and cannot prove, that needing something makes it false. It does not. Hunger does not prove there is no such thing as bread. The longing for water in a desert is not evidence against the existence of water. The fact that we desperately want the new creation tells you nothing, by itself, about whether it is real. And Christianity, crucially, does not finally rest its hope on how much we need it. It rests it somewhere far more exposed and far more checkable. It rests it on a tomb that was found empty on a Sunday morning, on the claim that a man who was truly dead was truly raised, not as a metaphor for the human spirit but as an event in history, the first piece of the new creation breaking backward into the old. Take away the resurrection and the whole hope collapses, and Paul says exactly that, that if Christ has not been raised our faith is worthless and we are still in our sins and to be pitied above all people. The Christian does not believe every tear will be wiped away because the world is unbearable otherwise. He believes it because he believes a grave came open, and if that is true, then the God who opened it can be trusted with the ending he has promised. So here is the turn, and it is the word the whole study has been walking toward, and it is a word Dietrich Bonhoeffer gave the church from a prison cell. Penultimate. Bonhoeffer distinguished the ultimate, the final word of God, from the penultimate, the next-to-last things that fill the time before it. And present suffering, all of it, everything this study has refused for five weeks to minimize, is penultimate. Hear both halves of that, because the whole thing depends on holding them together. Penultimate does not mean unreal. The pain is not nothing, and I have fought every session against the lie that it is nothing, against the cheap answer and the forced smile and the formula that turns grief into growth. The suffering is real, and it is the next-to-last word, and the next-to-last word is a genuine word, spoken over genuine lives, and it hurts exactly as much as it hurts. But it is not the last word. There is a last word coming, and it is not spoken by death, and it is not spoken by the disease or the grave or the abandonment. It is spoken by the God who bends down himself to dry the face of everyone who ever wept. Not yet. That is the honest part, and it is why we still grieve, why the tears are still real and still falling and still allowed. But surely. That is the other part, and it is why, Paul says, we do not grieve as those who have no hope. Not without grief. As those who grieve, and hope, at the same time, holding the wound and the promise in one hand, refusing to let go of either, until the day the hand that was pierced reaches out and wipes the last tear away.

scriptureStudy.note: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people. The hope is not our escape to God's place but God's coming to ours, the end of exile, which is why the new creation honors this world and body rather than discarding them.

He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more. Every tear, not most, and the hand that wipes them is God's own, an intimate act of the same God who wept at a tomb, now bending to every grieving face.

He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord God will wipe away tears from all faces. Centuries before Revelation, Isaiah sees the same ending, death not merely defeated but swallowed up, and God himself drying every face, so the hope is woven through the whole of Scripture.

The sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us. Paul does not say the sufferings are small, he says they are outweighed, held in the balance against a glory so great that the comparison, not the pain, is what fails.

The whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. Paul names the present suffering as labor, real and painful, but oriented toward a birth, which is the penultimate held together with the ultimate in a single image.

The last enemy to be destroyed is death. Death is named an enemy, not a natural friend or a doorway to be welcomed, and its destruction is promised as certain, which is why grief is honest and despair is not.

That you may not grieve as others do who have no hope. Paul does not forbid grief, he transforms it. The Christian still weeps, fully and honestly, but not as one for whom the tears are the final word, holding sorrow and hope together.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the shape of the Christian hope, because it is widely misunderstood even inside the church, and recovering it changes how a group carries present pain. N. T. Wright, in Surprised by Hope, published in 2008, argues at length that the New Testament's hope is not the popular picture of disembodied souls going to heaven, but resurrection and new creation, the renewal of heaven and earth and the raising of the body, and that the church's drift toward a purely spiritual, escapist heaven has weakened both its comfort and its engagement with the present world. A group should weigh this carefully against the sentimental version most have absorbed, and notice how much more seriously the biblical hope takes the goodness of creation, the reality of the body, and therefore the genuine wrongness of the suffering that assaults them, because a hope that discards the world cannot mourn its wounds as Scripture does. Set this beside Dietrich Bonhoeffer's distinction between the ultimate and the penultimate, worked out in his Ethics, which gives the group language for holding present suffering as real and serious, a genuine next-to-last word, without letting it become final. Then take up the hardest pastoral question this session raises, and take it with great care, because the hope of the new creation must never be used as a weapon against present grief. There is a way of deploying heaven that silences the sufferer, that tells the bereaved to stop crying because it will all be fine someday, and this is a real and cruel misuse that the study has fought against for five weeks and must not commit at the end. The biblical hope does the opposite. It gives grief its full permission now, because it takes seriously that the thing lost was good and its loss is genuinely evil, and it refuses despair, because it insists the loss is not the last word. A group should sit with how to hold both, the not yet that keeps grief honest and the surely that keeps it from collapsing into hopelessness, and should be especially watchful, in a study on suffering, for anyone whose pain has moved toward despair that will not lift or toward wanting to be gone, making sure such a person is met not with a verse alone but with real help, a pastor, a counselor, a doctor, a crisis line, and the plain assurance that reaching for that help is not a failure of faith but an act of it. The aim is to end the whole study where the Bible ends, not with the suffering explained, but with the suffering neither minimized nor made final, held under the promise of the God who will wipe every tear away with his own hand.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group lost his wife two years ago and has, in his own words, made a kind of peace with never being happy again, a quiet and settled hopelessness that he does not even present as a crisis, because to him it is simply realism. When the session speaks of the new creation, he says, without drama, that he finds it hard to believe and is not sure he wants to, because hoping again feels like it would betray his grief or set him up to be crushed a second time. Here is the work for the leader, and it must be gentle, unhurried, and watchful. Do not argue him into hope, and do not treat his grief as a problem to be solved by a verse, because his love for his wife is real and his sorrow is honest and neither should be rushed. Grant that hoping again is genuinely frightening, and that his fear of betraying her memory comes from love, not faithlessness. Then, carefully, offer him the shape the study has been building, that the hope of the new creation is not a betrayal of his grief but its vindication, because it promises that the wife he lost was so good that God himself will undo her loss, and that holding hope does not require him to grieve less but frees him to grieve without despair. Do not press him toward a feeling he cannot manufacture. But be watchful too, because a settled hopelessness after a great loss can be closer to danger than it appears, and if there is any sign that his despair has moved toward not wanting to be here, meet it directly and kindly, make sure he is not carrying it alone, and connect him to a pastor or counselor without shaming him for needing one. The gift you can offer is not a demand that he feel hopeful, but the company of a God, and a group, who will hold both his grief and the promise in the same hand until the day he can hold them himself.

memoryVerse.text: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.

leaderPrimer: The particular danger of a study on suffering is that it can go wrong in two opposite directions, and a good leader has to watch both at once. It can become an intellectual seminar, a room of people solving the problem of pain as an equation while the actual sufferer among them feels more alone with every clever point, or it can collapse into a grief that circles without hope, where the pain is honored so thoroughly that no one dares mention the resurrection. Neither is the aim. The aim is a room where the suffering is fully real and the hope is fully real, held together, neither one canceling the other, which is the hardest and truest place to stand. So set the tone the first night and hold it. This is not a debate to be won. It is a wound to be borne together, and the person in the most pain in the room sets the pace, not the person with the most to say. Refuse the cheap answers out loud, name them early, everything happens for a reason, God needed another angel, at least it was not worse, so that everyone knows this room does not run on them. And when someone shares real grief, resist with everything in you the urge to fix it, and teach the room to resist it too, because the impulse to explain another person's pain is almost always the impulse to flee it. The most spiritual thing said in these five weeks may be nothing at all, a hand on a shoulder, a shared silence, a leader willing to sit in the ash heap rather than stand over it. Now the part that is not optional. In any group studying suffering, there is a real chance that someone present is in acute grief, or in a despair that has grown dangerous, or is quietly wondering whether they want to still be here. Watch for it. Know, before you begin, how you would respond, and have real resources ready, a pastor, a counselor, a physician, a crisis line you can name and hand over. If anyone signals that their pain has turned toward self-harm or toward not wanting to live, do not treat it as a discussion point and do not leave it to a verse. Meet it directly and kindly, stay with them, make sure they are not alone, and connect them to real help that day, and say plainly that reaching for that help is not a failure of faith but an act of it. Keep the path to help visible in every session, not just the last. Bell leads this from inside it, not above it. He came to faith out of atheism partly over this very question, he was raised without a father, he has buried people he loved and sat with people who wanted to die, and he does not pretend to stand on the far side of suffering dispensing answers. If you present yourself as the one who has it resolved, the room will perform a resolution it does not feel and nothing will move. Go in as a fellow sufferer who is still holding on, still being carried more than carrying. Five weeks will not answer the problem of pain, and if you promise that, you will fail. What five weeks can do is send a hurting person home less alone, having learned that God permits the honest question, that lament is faithful speech, that the cross means he entered the dark first, that his grace can be sufficient in the thorn he does not remove, and that the last word over every tear is his own hand, wiping it away. That is not a solution. It is a company, and a hope, and for a person in pain it is more than enough to be going on with.

faq.q: Is this study going to try to explain why God allows suffering?
faq.a: No, and that is deliberate. The study takes the problem of pain with complete seriousness, states the atheist objection at its full strength, and then declines to do the one thing everyone expects, hand over a tidy explanation, because Scripture itself declines to. In the book of Job, God never tells Job the reason for his suffering. He gives Job himself instead, an encounter rather than an argument, and Job, who had demanded answers, goes quiet not because he was silenced but because he was met. The study follows that lead. Its claim is not that suffering has a satisfying explanation we can carry to a hospital room, but that God's final response to pain was not a theory but a participation, the cross, where he entered the darkness himself, and a promise, the new creation, where he wipes every tear away with his own hand. The study offers company and hope in the pain, not a solution to it, because the second is not honestly available and the first is what a sufferer actually needs.

faq.q: What if someone in the group is in deep grief, or in a despair that has become dangerous?
faq.a: Take it with complete seriousness, because in a study on suffering it is a real possibility, and the study is built to make room for it rather than paper over it. The leader primer urges every facilitator, before beginning, to know how they would respond and to have real resources ready, a pastor, a counselor, a physician, a crisis line that can be named and handed over. Watch the room, especially the quiet person, and keep the path to help visible in every session rather than only the last. If anyone signals that their pain has turned toward self-harm or toward not wanting to live, do not treat it as a discussion point and do not answer it with a verse alone. Meet it directly and kindly, stay with them, make sure they are not alone, and connect them to real help that day, and say plainly that reaching for that help is not a failure of faith but an act of it. The God at the center of this study wept at a grave. He does not ask anyone to suffer alone, and neither should the group.

faq.q: Does the study say it is wrong to ask God why, or to be angry with him?
faq.a: The opposite. Session one shows that in the book of Job, God rebuked the friends who defended him with tidy explanations and commended Job, who protested and demanded a hearing to God's face. Session two recovers lament, the fact that roughly a third of the Psalms are complaints God put in his people's mouths on purpose, how long O Lord and why have you forsaken me among them, and that Jesus himself prayed the opening line of a lament from the cross. So the honest question is not a threat to faith but often its truest form, the refusal to make peace with a lie in order to look pious. What the study asks is only that the question be aimed at God rather than away from him, brought into the relationship rather than used to end it, because that is the difference between lament, which keeps holding on, and grumbling, which quietly lets go. Bringing God your anger is not weak faith. It takes more faith to say the true thing to him than to bury it and offer him a polite distance.

faq.q: Is this study going to be too heavy or depressing to sit through?
faq.a: It is honest, which is not the same as depressing. The study refuses to minimize suffering, but it refuses despair just as firmly, and it holds the two together on purpose, the pain fully real and the hope fully real at the same time. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the ache it opened, every one moves toward the God who entered the dark and the promise that the dark does not get the last word. The final session lands not on the suffering but on the new creation, where God himself wipes away every tear. People in pain generally do not find honesty depressing, they find it a relief, because most of them have been carrying grief in rooms that had no place for it, and a study that will finally name the hard thing out loud, and then hold hope over it without cheapening either, tends to lift a weight rather than add one. It is heavy the way a real conversation is heavy, and light the way company in the dark is light.

faq.q: What does the study mean when it says the cross is God's answer to suffering?
faq.a: It means that Christianity's deepest response to the question where was God when it hurt is not a theory but a place, a cross. The study, drawing on the theologian Jurgen Moltmann and his book The Crucified God, shows that God did not stay above human suffering explaining it from a safe distance, but entered it himself in Christ, crying out the prayer of the forsaken from within real abandonment. This does not explain suffering, and the study is careful to say so. What it does is deeper and, in a hospital room, better, it means that when you go down into the dark, you do not go where God has never been. He went there first, at the cross, and by his Spirit he is there still. A God who cannot suffer cannot love, because love that risks and feels nothing is not love. The marks on Christ's hands are the permanent sign that God does not stay away from pain but enters it, so the sufferer is not alone in a place God avoids but accompanied in a place God has already been.

faq.q: Does the study teach that suffering is good for us, or that it makes us better people?
faq.a: No, and it works hard against exactly that formula, which it names as false and often cruel. Session four draws a careful line the church frequently blurs. There is a world of difference between saying suffering produces good, which is a lie, and saying God can bring good out of suffering, which is the testimony of people who have walked through the dark and come out still holding on. Suffering does not automatically produce anything good, it frequently produces bitterness and ruin, and to tell a grieving person their pain is building their character is an offense, not a comfort. The study points to Paul, who begged God three times to remove his thorn and was told no, not this will make sense later, just my grace is sufficient for you. The claim is never that the thorn was good. It is that God's grace was sufficient in it, a hope that can only be discovered from the inside, in the past tense, by the sufferer, and never imposed from outside on someone still bleeding.

faq.q: Is the hope of heaven in the last session just wishful thinking to make people feel better?
faq.a: The study takes that suspicion seriously rather than dodging it, because a hope too fragile to be questioned is not worth holding. It grants that a comfort can be invented precisely because it is needed. But it makes a careful point, that needing something does not make it false, hunger does not prove there is no bread, and that Christianity does not finally rest its hope on human need but on a claim about an event, the empty tomb, the resurrection asserted as history rather than metaphor, the first piece of the new creation breaking into the old. You can dispute that claim, and serious people do, but it is a claim about something that either happened or did not, not a wish dressed as a fact. The Christian does not believe every tear will be wiped away because the world is unbearable otherwise. He believes it because he believes a grave came open on a Sunday morning, and if that is true, the God who opened it can be trusted with the ending he has promised.

faq.q: The study keeps refusing cheap answers. Does that mean it has no answers at all?
faq.a: It has a great deal to say, but it refuses to say the things that are false, which is different from having nothing to offer. What it refuses are the cheap answers that ease the speaker's discomfort at the sufferer's expense, everything happens for a reason offered in the first raw week, God needed another angel, at least it was not worse, and the formula that turns pain into a guaranteed growth program. What it offers instead is harder and truer, the permission to bring the honest question to God, the recovery of lament as faithful speech, the cross where God entered the dark himself, grace proved sufficient in the thorn that is not removed, and the promise that suffering is penultimate and not final because God will wipe away every tear with his own hand. Those are not evasions, they are the deepest things the faith actually holds. The study simply refuses to pretend it has a neat explanation for any particular person's pain, because it does not, and pretending would be the real failure to answer.

faq.q: What does penultimate mean, and why does the study end on that word?
faq.a: Penultimate means next-to-last, and the study borrows it from Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who distinguished the ultimate, God's final word, from the penultimate, the things that fill the time before it. Present suffering, the study says, is penultimate, and holding that word rightly requires both halves at once. Penultimate does not mean unreal, the pain is genuine and the study has refused for five weeks to minimize it. But penultimate does mean not final, because there is a last word coming that suffering does not get to speak. The study ends here because it is the honest place to end, holding the not yet and the surely together. The not yet is why we still grieve, honestly and fully, the tears real and allowed. The surely is why we do not grieve as those who have no hope. Both at once, neither canceling the other, until the day the hand that was pierced reaches out and wipes the last tear away.

faq.q: Why does the writer keep putting himself inside the study instead of just teaching it?
faq.a: Because that is the method, and the method matters. The writer came to faith out of atheism partly over the problem of suffering, was raised without a father, and has buried people he loved and sat with people who wanted to die, and he refuses to stand on the far side of pain dispensing answers he has not had to live. He admits to praying the prayer that was met with silence, to handing a grieving person a sentence he later wished he could take back, to wanting a God too strong to be wounded. He writes from inside the room, not above it, and he asks every leader to do the same, because you cannot sit well with a sufferer while pretending you have never bled. A study on suffering led by someone who has it all resolved would be unbearable and false. By keeping the writer inside the pain rather than above it, the study makes honest company possible, which is the only thing that actually helps a person in the dark.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is not this just religion offering comfort it cannot back up?
faq.a: It is a fair suspicion, and the study earns the right to answer it by stating your objection at full strength before responding, in your own voice rather than a straw version. It grants that the problem of pain is the strongest case against God, that much suffering is genuinely undeserved, and that a comfort can be invented because it is needed. It does not pretend the question is stupid, because the writer once asked it himself as an unbeliever. What it offers is not a proof that resolves the problem, but a claim you can weigh, that the God in question did not stay above suffering explaining it from a distance, but entered it at the cross, and that the hope of a world made new rests not on wishful thinking but on the assertion that a tomb was found empty. You do not have to accept that to notice that Christianity's answer to suffering is stranger and more costly than the caricature, a God who wept and bled rather than one who watched untroubled. The study leaves you able to disagree and keep thinking, which is the most it should do, and more than the cliches ever did.

faq.q: Someone I love is suffering right now. Can I use this to help me sit with them?
faq.a: Yes, and in some ways that is exactly who it is for. The study is as much about how to be present to another person's pain as about how to bear your own, and its most repeated lesson is the one that helps a companion most, resist the urge to explain or fix. The single most common way we fail the suffering is by reaching for a sentence that eases our own discomfort and leaves them more alone, and the study names that impulse honestly, because the writer confesses to it himself. What it teaches instead is to sit in the ash heap rather than stand over it, to let the hard question be asked, to weep with those who weep, and to keep the path to real help visible when the pain is more than you can carry with them. You do not need to have answers to be present, and the study will free you from thinking you do. The most loving thing you can often do for someone in pain is to stay, to say less, and to refuse to leave, which is precisely what God did at the cross.

timeline.event: The book of Job is composed, the Bible's own sharpest statement of the problem of pain, in which a righteous man suffers for no reason he is ever told, protests to God's face, and is commended for it while his friends who explained his suffering are rebuked.

Jerusalem falls to Babylon and the temple is destroyed, and the book of Lamentations gives the exiled people a scripted grief, five poems of raw sorrow that still turn, in their middle, to the steadfast love of the Lord that never ceases.

Jesus is crucified, crying from the cross the opening line of a lament psalm, my God my God why have you forsaken me, and God himself enters the godforsakenness that the whole problem of pain is made of, answering suffering by participation rather than explanation.

Augustine develops the influential account of evil as privation, a lack or corruption of the good rather than a thing in itself, shaping Western Christian reflection on suffering and evil for more than a millennium, for both insight and limitation.

The philosopher Gottfried Leibniz publishes his Theodicy, coining the word for the justification of God in the face of evil and arguing that ours is the best of all possible worlds, a confident optimism the century would not leave standing.

An earthquake destroys Lisbon on All Saints Day while the churches are full, shocking the European conscience and prompting Voltaire to turn the disaster into a weapon against Leibniz's optimism, first in a poem and then in the satire of Candide.

C. S. Lewis publishes The Problem of Pain, a careful intellectual defense of belief in God in the face of suffering, arguing among other things that pain is God's megaphone to rouse a deaf world, a book he would later find harder to live than to write.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer is executed by the Nazis, having written from prison, in the months before, that only a suffering God can help, a line drawn not from a comfortable study but from a cell, and his Ethics gives the church the language of the ultimate and the penultimate.

C. S. Lewis publishes A Grief Observed after watching his wife die of cancer, a raw journal that reads at times like it is arguing with his own earlier book, and shows that an answer which satisfies in the study can shatter at the graveside.

Jurgen Moltmann publishes The Crucified God, arguing that God is not the impassive spectator of human suffering but the one who took it into his own being at the cross, so that there is no depth of human abandonment where God has not already been.

Nicholas Wolterstorff publishes Lament for a Son after his twenty-five-year-old son died in a climbing accident, refusing every consolation that would make the death smaller and insisting that faith is not the absence of the wound but the trust that keeps holding on inside it.

Timothy Keller publishes Walking with God through Pain and Suffering, surveying how cultures have tried to make sense of pain and arguing that the Christian account refuses both to minimize suffering as illusion and to treat it as meaningless.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here, because it takes courage to talk honestly about suffering in a room. Before we start, a few things. First, this is not a debate to be won, it is a hard thing we are going to carry together, and the person in the most pain here sets the pace, not the person with the most to say. Second, we are not going to run on the cheap answers in this room, the everything happens for a reason and the God needed another angel and the at least it could be worse, so if one slips out, we will gently set it down and keep going. Third, when someone here shares something real, the job is not to fix it, it is to hear it, and I will be resisting the urge to explain your pain and I will ask you to resist it for each other too, because sitting with someone beats solving them. And what is said in honesty stays in this room. One more thing, and I mean it plainly. Suffering is heavy, and if anyone here is carrying something that has grown too dark to hold alone, whether that is grief that will not lift or a place where you have wondered whether you want to still be here, please tell me, tonight or privately, because you do not have to carry that by yourself and I will help you find real help. The God we are going to talk about wept at a grave. He does not ask anyone to suffer alone. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what this session says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the actual grief or fear each of us walked in carrying, because none of this matters if it stays a discussion about suffering in general.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not resolved, because suffering is not a problem solved in an evening and the study does not tie a bow on it either. Take the weight of this home with you rather than setting it down at the door. Try the practice this week, in your own life, even haltingly. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And come back ready to be honest, not finished. Before we go, remember what I said at the start, my door is open if any of you is carrying something too heavy tonight, and there is no shame at all in reaching for help. Let me pray for us, and then I will see you next time. Thank you for the courage it took to be in this conversation.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about not fixing each other and refusing the cheap answers, name the resources for anyone in crisis, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, The Question We Are Not Allowed to Ask, full discussion and practice, with extended time on Job and the protest tradition.
Week 3: Session 2, Permission to Complain to God, praying a lament psalm together and sitting with the church's lost language of grief.
Week 4: Session 3, A God Who Does Not Explain, but Comes, part one, reading the cross as God's entry into godforsakenness.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, the objection that a suffering God is a weak God, and the pastoral turn that we never go into the dark where God has not been first.
Week 6: Session 4, The Thorn That Was Not Removed, with care taken to refuse the formula and honor the unhealed.
Week 7: Session 5, Every Tear, and Whose Hand Wipes It, the new creation and suffering as penultimate.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and what each person is carrying home, closing in the promise of the God who wipes every tear away.

Week 4: Session 5, Every Tear, and Whose Hand Wipes It, plus a short integration close in the hope of the new creation.

bibliography.title: Walking with God through Pain and Suffering
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: The pastoral spine of the whole study, surveying how cultures have tried to make sense of pain and arguing that the Christian account refuses both to minimize suffering and to treat it as meaningless. Anchors sessions 1 and 4.

bibliography.title: The Crucified God
bibliography.author: Jurgen Moltmann
bibliography.note: The theological center of session 3, arguing that God took human suffering into his own being at the cross so that no depth of abandonment is beyond his reach. Written by a man who found faith as a prisoner of war. Leader to handle its harder claims about God's suffering with care.

bibliography.title: The Problem of Pain
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: The classic intellectual defense of belief in God in the face of suffering, useful for stating the questions of session 1 clearly. Best read alongside A Grief Observed, since Lewis himself found the answers harder to live than to write.

bibliography.title: A Grief Observed
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis's raw journal after his wife's death, which reads at times like it argues with his own earlier book, invaluable for the honesty of sessions 1 and 2 and the difference between an answer in the study and a grief at the graveside.

bibliography.title: Lament for a Son
bibliography.author: Nicholas Wolterstorff
bibliography.note: A father's meditation after the death of his adult son, refusing every consolation that would make the loss smaller, a moving witness for sessions 2 and 5. Not a systematic text, offered as accompaniment for the grieving.

bibliography.title: The Doors of the Sea: Where Was God in the Tsunami?
bibliography.author: David Bentley Hart
bibliography.note: A short, bracing meditation on God and catastrophic suffering written after the 2004 tsunami, refusing both the tidy theodicy and the atheist despair. Background for session 1. Leader to weigh its dense argument before pressing specific claims.

bibliography.title: The Cross of Christ
bibliography.author: John Stott
bibliography.note: A rich treatment of the cross, including Stott's famous witness that he could not believe in God were it not for the cross and a God who entered our pain. Supports session 3. Leader to confirm specific quotations before attributing them.

bibliography.title: Night
bibliography.author: Elie Wiesel
bibliography.note: The memoir of the Nazi camps that Moltmann draws on in The Crucified God, including the searing scene of the child on the gallows. A witness from outside the faith to the depth of the problem, to be handled with reverence for the suffering it records.

bibliography.title: Letters and Papers from Prison
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Bonhoeffer's writings from a Nazi cell, including the line that only a suffering God can help, essential background for session 3 and, with his Ethics, the source of the ultimate and penultimate of session 5.

bibliography.title: Surprised by Hope
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: A recovery of the biblical hope as resurrection and new creation rather than escape to a disembodied heaven, the framework behind session 5. Leader to confirm specific claims before pressing them as the study's own.

bibliography.title: Job
bibliography.author: the book of Job
bibliography.note: The primary text of session 1 and the Bible's own sharpest statement of the problem of pain, to be read and not merely cited, ending not with an explanation but with an encounter.

bibliography.title: The Book of Psalms
bibliography.author: the psalmists of Israel
bibliography.note: The songbook a third full of laments that grounds session 2, teaching the church its lost language of grief. Psalms 13, 22, 42, and 88 in particular, to be prayed and not only studied.

furtherReading: Walking with God through Pain and Suffering, Timothy Keller, for those who want the fuller pastoral and cross-cultural case behind sessions 1 and 4.
A Grief Observed, C. S. Lewis, for anyone in fresh grief who needs to see honesty and faith held together on the same page, read alongside the study's recovery of lament.
Lament for a Son, Nicholas Wolterstorff, for those willing to sit with a father's unhealed grief and what it shows about trust that keeps holding on inside the wound.
The Crucified God, Jurgen Moltmann, for readers ready for the demanding theological case that God entered suffering himself, read with care for its harder claims.
Job, read straight through, for anyone willing to watch the Bible refuse the tidy answer and end instead in an encounter with the God who does not explain.

glossary.definition: The attempt to justify God in the face of evil and suffering, to show how a good and powerful God can be squared with a world of pain. A word coined by Leibniz in 1710. The study takes the problem seriously but, like Job, declines to offer a tidy theodicy as the answer.

The oldest and heaviest objection to belief in God, that a world with this much undeserved suffering is hard to square with a God who is both perfectly good and fully able to stop it. Stated by the study at full strength before any response is offered.

Faithful speech that brings grief, protest, and accusation directly to God while continuing to hold on to him, the scripted language of roughly a third of the Psalms. Distinct from grumbling, which talks about God to others and lets go of him.

The strand of Scripture, running through Job, the lament psalms, Jeremiah, and Habakkuk, that puts the hard question to God to his face and is commended rather than rebuked for it, proving that honest anguish addressed to God is a form of faith, not its failure.

The condition of abandonment by God, the depth the problem of pain reaches, into which, at the cross, God himself entered in Christ, who cried out my God my God why have you forsaken me, so that no forsaken person is anywhere God has not already been.

The classical conviction that God in his divine nature cannot suffer or change, held to guard God's perfection and freedom. The study weighs it honestly against the modern claim that a God who cannot suffer cannot love, and holds the tension rather than collapsing it.

Jurgen Moltmann's phrase for the God who did not stay above human suffering explaining it from a distance, but took it into his own being at the cross, revealing a power that is made perfect in weakness and a love willing to be wounded.

Paul's name for the unnamed affliction he begged God three times to remove, and did not have removed. The Bible never says what it was, a mercy that lets every sufferer with an unhealed wound find themselves in Paul's, and hear the answer given him.

God's answer to Paul's prayer for relief, my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. Not the removal of the thorn or an explanation of it, but a grace given in it, and a strength that shows up precisely in the place of weakness.

The biblical hope, not escape to a disembodied heaven but heaven coming down, a renewed heaven and earth where God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear with his own hand. The last word over all suffering, grounded in the resurrection.

Bonhoeffer's word for the next-to-last things that fill the time before God's final word, the ultimate. Present suffering is penultimate, real and serious and genuinely painful, and yet not final, because there is a last word coming that suffering does not get to speak.

The two things a sufferer might be offered, and the study's insistence that God mostly gives the first rather than the second, presence rather than a reason, company in the dark rather than an account of why the dark is there.

Hebrew for steadfast, covenant love, the faithful loving-kindness of God that Lamentations 3 clings to in the middle of grief, declaring it never ceases and is new every morning, the ground of hope that the sufferer calls to mind alongside the affliction, not instead of it.

God's sovereign governing of all things, including what he permits to wound us. The study holds it carefully, refusing both the formula that reads every pain as a coded blessing and the despair that reads God's permission of suffering as his absence from it.
